summary: Defines YANG Schema Item iDentifiers (SIDs), globally unique 63-bit unsigned integers identifying YANG items compactly for constrained environments. It covers semantics, registration, and assignment processes for IETF-managed YANG modules.

eli5.summary: Long names take lots of space. This gives each item in a YANG model a short number, like a library card number, to save room.

questions: what is a sid file in yang
subtitle: Short, globally unique numbers that stand in for long YANG names, plus the registries and file format that keep them consistent.

tldr.problem: NETCONF and RESTCONF identify YANG items by name, which is too bulky for constrained devices and networks. A compact identifier is only useful if every party agrees on which number means which name.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG SID is a globally unique 63-bit unsigned integer that maps to exactly one YANG name. SIDs are handed out in registered ranges, recorded in a JSON ".sid" file, and IANA runs three new registries for the IETF-managed part of the space.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the rules for assigning and registering SIDs, the ".sid" file format and its YANG module, and the IANA registries, a media type and a CoAP Content-Format.

today: RFC 9595 is a Proposed Standard, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the SID rules, the ".sid" file format and the IANA registries for IETF-managed YANG modules.

sections.title: Why YANG Needs Compact Identifiers
sections.content:
YANG (RFC 7950) items such as data nodes and identities need unique identifiers. In NETCONF and RESTCONF (RFC 8040) those identifiers are names. To use YANG-modeled data in constrained devices and constrained networks, a more compact method is required. That compact identifier is the YANG Schema Item iDentifier, or YANG SID, encoded as a 63-bit unsigned integer. The 63-bit limit makes SIDs easier to handle on platforms that lack 64-bit unsigned arithmetic, and losing one bit of range is not significant.

SIDs identify identities, data nodes, RPCs and their inputs and outputs, actions and their inputs and outputs, notifications, and YANG modules and features. They are especially useful for a compact encoding of YANG-CBOR (RFC 9254).

SIDs are globally unique integers, guaranteed by a registration system. They are registered in blocks called SID ranges. Once considered stable, SIDs are assigned permanently, and items added by a new module revision are added to the SIDs already assigned.
sections.eli5: Writing out a long name every time is like spelling your whole address on every note. A short number saves space, as long as everyone agrees whose number it is.

sections.title: Objectives for SID Assignment
sections.content:
The overriding goal is global interoperability of protocols that use SIDs to talk about YANG-modeled data. That requires SIDs to stay stable without hindering the evolution of the modules they describe. The RFC states three technical objectives:

  • Objective 1 (MUST): any 63-bit unsigned integer is either unassigned as a SID or immutably maps to exactly one YANG name. Only the move from unassigned to that mapping is defined.
  • Objective 2 (SHOULD): any YANG name in active use has one SID assigned, so there are no names without SIDs and no names with several SIDs.
  • Objective 3 (MUST): the SID management system is independent of any module versioning.

The RFC admits Objective 2 cannot be fully attained, because names are not necessarily born with a SID and because entirely autonomous entities might assign SIDs for the same name without communicating, "like ships in the night". Further goals include keeping short SIDs (2 to 4 bytes) readily available while using the vast 63-bit space for permissionless actions, and keeping assignments local so the SID delta mechanism stays efficient.
sections.eli5: The big rule is that one number never means two different things. A second wish is that each thing gets just one number.

sections.title: Parties and Roles
sections.content:
Besides the existing parties around a YANG module (module controller, registration entity, module repository and module user), SID handling adds four roles. A SID assigner assigns SIDs for a module. A SID range registry supplies assigners with SID ranges. A SID repository supplies assignments to users, usually as a ".sid" file. A SID user is the module user who uses the SIDs.

The desired end state is that the module developer is the SID assigner, the module repository is the SID repository, and the module user is the SID user. The RFC calls a controller who does this a type-1, "SID-guiding" module controller. A type-2 ("SID-aware") controller has heard of SIDs and can designate a SID assigner instead. A type-3 ("SID-oblivious") controller is not assigning SIDs at all, so module repositories can act as mediators and offer a carefully chosen assigner.

For modules still in development, assigners decide whether to reassign SIDs from scratch ("clean slate") or build on a previous revision. Once a module is declared stable, its SID assignments SHOULD be declared stable too.
sections.eli5: Think of a school that hands out locker numbers. Someone gives out blocks of numbers, someone assigns them to students, and someone keeps the list so everyone can look it up.

sections.title: The ".sid" File Lifecycle
sections.content:
An author who wants SIDs first obtains a SID range from a registry, uses it to assign or generate SIDs for the module's items, and stores the result in a ".sid" file. Many YANG modules never need this, since NETCONF and RESTCONF work without SIDs. Registering the ".sid" file is optional but recommended, to promote interoperability and avoid duplicate allocation.

During development, provisional assignments are marked unstable, so they can be removed and the number reused. When the specification becomes a final document, they are marked stable. Tooling should offer two variants: a "published" file with only stable assignments, and an "unpublished" file that also contains unstable ones.

Each time a module, an imported module or an included submodule changes, a new ".sid" file MAY be created if the new items need SIDs, preferably with an automated tool. All SIDs in the previous file that was in active use MUST be present in the new one. If more SIDs are needed than were allocated, a new range MUST be added to assignment-range.
sections.eli5: While a recipe is still being tested, the numbers on it are written in pencil. Once the recipe is final, they are written in pen and never erased.

sections.title: The ".sid" File Format
sections.content:
A ".sid" file persists and publishes the SIDs for one YANG module. The file is encoded as JSON using the rules of RFC 7951, and its structure is defined by the YANG module ietf-sid-file, which uses the sx:structure extension from RFC 8791.

The top level holds module-name, optional module-revision, sid-file-version and description, a sid-file-status of unpublished or published, a list of dependency-revision entries for imported modules, a list of assignment-range entries and a list of item entries.

Each assignment-range has an entry-point (the lowest SID available) and a size, and ranges MUST NOT overlap. Each item has a status (stable, unstable or obsolete), a namespace (module, identity, feature or data), an identifier and a sid. For the data namespace the identifier is a schema-node path. The list MUST include an entry for each item the module defines. A published file MUST NOT contain unstable items, and for any one SID the status can only move from unstable to stable, and possibly from stable to obsolete.
sections.eli5: The file is a phone book for one module. Each line pairs a name with its number, and the top of the page says which block of numbers the module may use.

sections.title: Automatic SID Assignment
sections.content:
Appendix B says SID assignment SHOULD be automated, and describes a recommended process. A tool extracts the module's items and sorts them alphabetically, with namespace entries in descending order and identifier entries in ascending order. SIDs are then assigned sequentially from the range's entry point. Sequential assignment minimizes serialization overhead, especially for protocols that send the delta between a reference SID and the current one. If the items outnumber the range, an extra range is added.

When a module in active use is updated, existing assignments are kept, only new items get new SIDs, and the ".sid" file version number is incremented. A renamed but structurally similar node MAY keep its old SID. If an item's meaning changes, a new SID MAY be assigned. If a data type change alters the CBOR encoding, a new SID is a significant help to implementations. Input and output items of an RPC or action MUST always get SIDs, because other modules can augment them.
sections.eli5: A machine hands out numbers one after another in alphabetical order, and when new items show up later it only gives them the next unused numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A SID maps a concept to an integer, so if the source of the mapping is not trusted, an attacker who controls it could create new risks. ".sid" files are expected to be processed by developers in a software development environment, who are advised to import them only from authoritative sources. IANA is the authoritative source for IETF-managed YANG modules.

Less constrained systems such as network management systems could also process these files and must take equal care. Because ".sid" files can use dereferenceable identifiers, which could lead an implementation to perform remote access automatically, an attacker could gain information about or control over such accesses, with security and privacy implications.
sections.eli5: If someone hands you a fake phone book, you could call the wrong people. So only use phone books from a source you trust.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Ranges
sections.content:
The RFC creates three registries. YANG-SID Mega-Ranges records delegation of a block of SIDs to a third party such as a standards body or registrar. The size SHOULD be one million SIDs, or in exceptional cases a multiple of that. The policy is Expert Review, and the initial entry gives IANA the block starting at 0 with size 1,000,000. IETF YANG-SID Ranges records the range assigned to each module. IETF YANG-SID Modules records the ".sid" file for each module, and its policy is Expert Review.

Within IANA's first million SIDs, 0 to 999 is IESG Approval (SID 0 is reserved for implementations to signal the absence of a SID and never appears in interchange). The ranges 1,000 to 59,999 and 100,000 to 299,999 are for YANG modules in RFCs. The range 60,000 to 99,999 is experimental and MUST NOT be used in operational deployments. The range 300,000 to 999,999 is reserved.

A module's range size is recommended to be a multiple of 50 and at least 33% above the current number of items, and SHOULD NOT exceed 1,000. A ".sid" file MUST NOT be published as part of an RFC, since the IANA registry is authoritative, with this RFC itself as an exception. The RFC also registers the media type application/yang-sid+json and assigns it CoAP Content-Format ID 260.
sections.eli5: IANA is like the town office that keeps the master list of who owns which block of numbers. Some blocks are for official use, some are for practice, and some are held back for later.
